reference_title: Design, Analysis, and Testing of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations that Support Transportation Facilities

sections.title: Construction Management and Inspection
sections.summary: Successful lateral load performance depends on achieving the minimum embedment depth, avoiding disturbance of near-surface geo-materials that provide lateral resistance, and building the foundation elements with the required structural integrity. Knowledgeable inspection, recognition of and response to unanticipated conditions, and clear communication between inspector and designer are essential. General driven pile inspection guidance is in Hannigan et al. (2016) and drilled shaft guidance is in Brown et al. (2010); this chapter addresses considerations specific to lateral loading.
sections.body: Successful construction of foundation elements to meet the design objectives for lateral load resistance depends on: (a) achieving the predetermined minimum embedment established by the designer; (b) avoiding disturbance of the geo-materials around the foundation element that are relied upon for providing resistance to lateral loads; and (c) constructing the foundation elements with the required structural strength and integrity. Knowledgeable supervision and inspection is essential, and equally important is the recognition of, and response to, unanticipated site conditions that could adversely impact the performance of the foundation to lateral loading. Inspection roles and responsibilities are discussed in detail in Hannigan et al. (2016) and Brown et al. (2010) for driven piles and drilled shafts, respectively. Construction management and inspection considerations with specific bearing upon laterally loaded foundations are discussed in the following sections.
key_points: Three keys to lateral performance: (1) minimum embedment depth, (2) no disturbance to near-surface soils, (3) structural integrity
Knowledgeable inspection and prompt response to unanticipated conditions are essential
Driven pile inspection: Hannigan et al. (2016); drilled shaft inspection: Brown et al. (2010)
sections.applicability: Construction management and inspection oversight for laterally loaded deep foundations

sections.title: Constructability Review
sections.summary: Before construction, the design should be reviewed to verify it is constructible with available means and methods. A constructability review addresses: foundation size and type appropriateness (pile dimensions, drilled shaft diameter for local contractor pool), site constraints (access, slopes, headroom), ability to reach required depth, installation risks (vibration settlement, excavation instability, contaminated spoils), third-party risks, and construction sequence feasibility. The review should be performed by staff with appropriate construction experience.
sections.body:
Prior to construction, the design should be reviewed to verify that the design is constructible with available means and methods. Elements of construction that may pose risks should be identified and mitigated if possible.

Considerations for a constructability review include: (1) Are the foundation size and type appropriate? For piles, are sizes and lengths appropriate for the pile type and will splicing impact the schedule? For drilled shafts, large diameters may be inappropriate on small local projects that attract only local contractors. (2) Can foundations be installed given site constraints such as working area, slopes, headroom, access, and equipment support? (3) Can the required depths be realized — can the bearing strata be penetrated to the required depth with the proposed foundation size and type? For driven piles, a driveability analysis should generally be performed. For drilled shafts, the need for specialty tools to penetrate hard layers should be considered. (4) Are there risks regarding installation such as settlement due to vibration, soil instability in excavations (drilled shafts, CFAs), contaminated spoils, etc.? (5) Are there risks to third parties, risks of damage to nearby structures, or community impacts? (6) Is the construction sequence technically and economically feasible? (7) Is there an area for load tests that is also representative of production foundation conditions? (8) Are there ways to resolve foreseeable problems efficiently? (9) For multiple viable alternatives, cost estimates and constructability comparison should be performed, recognizing that the apparent lowest-cost alternative may become more expensive if a higher-risk condition is encountered during construction.

Constructability review scope varies by project size, location, and local practice. The review should be performed by staff with appropriate construction experience.
key_points: Verify foundation size/type is appropriate for local contractor pool and project scale before construction
Confirm required depths can be achieved — driveability analysis for piles; specialty tool planning for drilled shafts in hard layers
Identify and mitigate installation risks: vibration-induced settlement, excavation instability, contaminated spoils, third-party impacts
Evaluate multiple alternatives on cost AND risk — apparent low-cost option may cost more if a higher-risk condition materializes
Constructability review must be performed by staff with appropriate construction experience
sections.applicability: Pre-construction design review for constructability of laterally loaded deep foundations

sections.title: Design Considerations and Changes in Construction
sections.summary: During construction, design may be impacted by: value engineering or contractor alternative design proposals (must demonstrate equivalent lateral load design criteria including required resistance factors); review and approval of contractor's means and methods (e.g., pre-excavation reduces lateral resistance within pre-excavated depth); and revised design triggered by construction data. Construction data that may require design re-evaluation includes weaker-than-anticipated soils, rock higher or lower than expected, and load test results. Design changes should be communicated promptly to the contractor.
sections.body:
As construction occurs, considerations, impacts, or changes to design may include:

(1) Proposed design changes based on data available before construction: value engineering or alternative design proposals by the contractor. This may require an entirely new design or a change in one aspect (pile type, drilled shaft size, etc.). The requirements for lateral load design — design specifications, Strength and Service Limit State deflections — should be clearly communicated to the contractor. Required or suggested resistance factors should also be communicated.

(2) Consideration of means and methods of construction: review and approval is typically part of the construction process. Pre-excavation for removal of obstructions may reduce the lateral resistance of soils within the depth of pre-excavation.

(3) Design changes due to data received in construction: subsurface condition data is received through additional explorations and actual construction operations. In design-bid-build, borings may be required at each shaft location to verify rock quality within socket depths; deferring investigation to construction introduces schedule and cost risk. In design-build, additional investigations are typically performed to develop or finalize the design. Examples of construction conditions requiring design re-evaluation include: (a) ground weaker than anticipated — lateral capacity must be re-evaluated and construction testing may be needed; (b) rock higher than anticipated tip depth — shorter pile/shaft may not satisfy lateral design requirements; rock sockets or pre-drilling into rock may be required; (c) rock lower than anticipated for socketed foundations — similar effect as weaker overlying material; (d) lateral load test results — design may be updated based on measured performance better or worse than anticipated.
key_points: Value engineering proposals must satisfy the same lateral load design criteria and resistance factors as the original design
Pre-excavation for obstructions reduces available lateral resistance within the depth of the pre-excavated zone
Deferring subsurface investigation to construction (design-bid-build) introduces significant schedule and cost risk
Rock higher than planned tip depth: shorter pile may not meet lateral design — rock socket or pre-drilling may be required
Construction load test results may trigger design update (better or worse performance than assumed)
sections.applicability: Managing design changes and construction data for laterally loaded deep foundations

sections.title: Driven Pile, Drilled Shaft, and Backfill Considerations
sections.summary: Foundation elements must be installed at design locations. Driven pile considerations: WEA drivability for hammer selection, top-to-bottom sequence on slopes, interior-first in groups, full-penetration splice welds, avoidance of jetting/pre-boring unless approved. Drilled shaft considerations: annular void backfill for oversized pre-drilling and surface casing, structural integrity testing (CSL per ASTM D6760, SE/IR per ASTM D5882), rock quality verification in sockets. Backfill must drain away from foundations; preloading before installation is recommended at soft soil sites.
sections.body:
Pile/shaft position and alignment: Laterally loaded foundations are designed based on planned spacing and overlap of passive influence zones using p-y multipliers. Foundations installed out of plan location or off vertical alignment violate the assumed group behavior. Clearing obstructions (abandoned foundations, tree roots, utilities) before installation reduces misalignment risk. All field adjustments to planned positions require engineer-of-record approval. Out-of-tolerance elements must be reported promptly.

Driven pile installations — equipment selection: Wave Equation Analysis (WEA) drivability studies assess hammer suitability for penetrating to the minimum tip elevation required for lateral resistance. WEA should be conducted by a knowledgeable foundation specialist matching the proposed driving system to pile type, ground conditions, and performance requirements.

Driving sequence: On slopes, drive sequentially from top to bottom; driving bottom-to-top causes displacement and tilting of previously installed piles. Within a pile group, drive interior piles first to prevent densification from precluding full penetration of exterior piles.

Driving refusal: When refusal occurs above plan minimum tip elevation due to hard layers, boulders, unanticipated rock, or densification from adjacent piles, notify the engineer-of-record. Corrective measures may include predrilling, spudding to break obstructions, changing the driving sequence, or modifying the group layout.

Splicing: Splices for steel piles should be full-penetration groove welds made by qualified certified welders. Mechanical splices with less than full bending strength should be avoided unless the splice can be located deep in the ground where bending moments are small. Field splices require engineer-of-record approval. Splices in precast concrete piles should generally be avoided.

Jetting and pre-boring: Where allowed, pre-bored hole diameter should not exceed the pile dimension by more than 6 inches (Hannigan et al. 2016). Both jetting and pre-boring reduce axial resistance and may also reduce lateral resistance by loosening soils around the pile; they should be avoided unless specifically allowed by project documents or approved by the engineer-of-record.

Drilled shafts — pre-drilling and surface casing: If pre-drill auger diameter exceeds the casing diameter, loosened material may be left outside the completed shaft. Pre-drilling should generally be limited to the shaft cut-off level or design scour depth; auger diameter should not exceed the completed shaft diameter. For oversized surface casing, the annular void must be filled with tamped granular backfill or grout. If permanent casing is used inside a surface casing, the annular void must be filled after permanent casing installation.

Structural integrity: Poor concrete placement can cause necking, honeycombing, soil intrusion, segregation, bleed-water channels, laitance, and cold joints — all of which reduce stiffness and lateral performance. NDT methods include Crosshole Sonic Logging (CSL) per ASTM D6760, Sonic Echo/Impulse Response (SE/IR) per ASTM D5882, Gamma-Gamma Logging (GGL) per Caltrans Test 233, and Thermal Integrity Profiling (TIP) per ASTM D7949.

Rock sockets: Variable rock surface elevation and quality can result in shaft lengths inconsistent with design assumptions. For highly loaded or non-redundant drilled shafts, rock core borings at each shaft location before drilling allow the designer to confirm or adjust the socket depth and the contractor to fabricate the reinforcing cage accordingly.

Backfill and grading: Embankments should generally be constructed before driving piles (pre-boring required for compacted fill). Where foundations must be installed before embankment, fill must be placed in small lifts with hand-operated compaction equipment. Backfill should slope to drain away from foundations. At sites with soft compressible soils, preloading before foundation installation is recommended to avoid lateral soil displacements from embankment construction causing pile bending.
key_points: All foundation position/alignment deviations must be reported to engineer-of-record; field adjustments require approval
WEA drivability analysis verifies hammer can drive pile to minimum lateral resistance tip elevation
Drive slope piles top-to-bottom; drive interior group piles first to prevent densification from blocking exterior piles
Refusal above plan tip elevation: notify engineer-of-record; consider predrilling, spudding, sequence change, or redesign
Steel pile splices: full-penetration groove welds; avoid mechanical splices near regions of high bending moment
Pre-drilling: limit auger to not more than 6 inches larger than pile; jetting and pre-boring reduce lateral resistance
Drilled shaft NDT: CSL per ASTM D6760, SE/IR per ASTM D5882, TIP per ASTM D7949 for structural integrity
Non-redundant/heavily loaded rock socket shafts: require rock core boring at each shaft location before drilling
Backfill around foundations must drain away; soft-soil sites should be preloaded before installing foundations
sections.applicability: Construction details for driven piles, drilled shafts, and site preparation to preserve lateral load performance
